articles.title: Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
articles.summary:
Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion

Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015.

Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5m, Saba reports.

He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376m.

The ministry put commercial losses above $85m and investment-sector losses above $20m.

Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350m in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period.

Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis.

The announcement provided no detailed methodology for the cumulative trillion-dollar estimate.

on

Knesset security chief tells Palestinian lawmaker to ‘take care of himself and be careful’

Ahmad Tibi, head of the Arab Movement for Change (Ta'al) party, speaks during an interview with AFP in the northern Israeli city of Nazareth on 2 November 2026 (Ahmad Gharabli/AFP)

Off

Palestinian lawmaker and Israeli citizen Ahmad Tibi is the most "threatened" member of Israel's parliament, according to the Knesset's security chief.

Israel Hayom reported on Monday that Tibi, a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List alliance, had been told to "take care of himself and be careful" by Yuval Chen, commander of the Knesset Guard, the security unit responsible for protecting Israel's parliament.

Chen reportedly told Tibi that he was “the most threatened member of the Knesset”. 

Sources in the Joint List accused the Knesset Guard of failing to provide adequate protection for Palestinian lawmakers inside the Knesset.

"Where are the Knesset Guard officers when they are needed? Why aren't they stationed permanently at the door of the Joint List during parliamentary group meetings?" they told the Israeli newspaper.

The warning to Tibi follows an incident on Monday in which Israeli comedian and right-wing figure Guy Hochman put his arms around the lawmaker while attempting to film a video.

Tibi pushed Hochman away after the comedian entered his personal space, prompting accusations that the Palestinian MP had assaulted him.

Hochman filed a complaint against Tibi with the Knesset Guard, alleging that the lawmaker had assaulted him. Ma'ariv also reported that a complaint against Tibi had been submitted to Israel's attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara.

Why Palestinian electoral gains in Israel cannot alter the racist structure of the state

Ghada Majadli

Read More »

Tibi, however, said he felt threatened when Hochman invaded his personal space on Knesset premises and that he had acted in self-defence.

"Hochman is a bad actor. He suddenly shoved a phone in my face, I pushed the phone away, and since then I've been told he went into intensive care," Tibi told Ma'ariv. 

Tibi said he had also filed a complaint against Hochman with the Knesset Guard, saying he had "felt threatened".

In a letter to the security unit, Tibi said Hochman had "approached me from behind, grabbed me without my consent, and shoved a phone to my face in an invasive and threatening manner".

"The incident is especially serious against the backdrop of the threats, incitement, and smears directed at me since the elections," the letter said.

It referred to the growing incitement against Tibi by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies since the Joint List and Ra'am won a historic 19 seats in the Knesset in last month's elections.

Anti-Palestinian incitement 

Tibi also accused the Knesset Guard of discriminating against Palestinian lawmakers.

"It is highly doubtful that an Arab man who behaved this way towards a Jewish minister would have received similar treatment, without the immediate intervention of the guards, who would have slammed him to the ground," he said.

"The security and dignity of Arab Knesset Members are not fair game," Tibi added, demanding an investigation into the incident.

Meanwhile, far-right Israeli politicians used the confrontation to launch fresh attacks against the Palestinian lawmaker. 

Israeli MP invokes internment of Japanese Americans in call to restrict Palestinian citizens

Read More »

Outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Jewish opposition parties, led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, not to form a government dependent on votes from the Joint List and Ra'am.

"This is what happens when they feel like the masters of the land; parliamentary violence turns into physical violence," Smotrich said, accusing Tibi of assaulting Hochman.

"The police must immediately open a criminal investigation against Ahmad Tibi," the settler leader added on X.

Two MPs from the party of outgoing National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, Otzma Yehudit, also attacked Tibi.

On Monday, Tally Gotliv stormed a Joint List parliamentary group meeting, while Hanamel Dorfman wrote on X: "The doctor of terror is also a doctor of violence."

Tibi is a qualified gynaecologist.

Tibi, who was elected last week as one of the Knesset's deputy speakers, has become a prominent target of the far-right incitement campaign against Palestinians in Israel since the elections.

He is not the only Palestinian to face such hostility.

Last week, a mosque in the village of Ed-Dahi was set on fire in a suspected arson attack linked to an Israeli mob.

articles.title: UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia
articles.summary:
UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia

Britain has imposed fresh sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis, accusing the group of “serious human rights abuses” and efforts to “undermine” Middle Eastern stability.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband linked the measures to attacks on merchant vessels in Bab al-Mandeb, saying they had “driven up the cost of living at home”.

He said the sanctions sent a “clear message” that Britain would “act in support of British values and interests,” according to a government statement.

“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.

The British government made no mention of its ally Saudi Arabia, which it is helping in an advisory role and with military hardware to carry out attacks on Yemen that have killed hundreds of civilians.

articles.title: Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
articles.summary:
Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won

Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 15:04

Lead counsel Arsalan Suleman tells Middle East Eye how the small African country took Myanmar to court and how survivor testimony helped secure a landmark judgement

Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats. 

They were about to deliver a landmark judgment in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the "crime of all crimes" as it has been described.

It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.

It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.

The case was brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.

In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.

But this time the question before the ICJ, the UN’s highest court which adjudicates mainly in disputes between states, was whether Myanmar itself, as a state actor, can be held responsible.

In 2017, Myanmar’s military burned Rohingya villages, carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.

More than 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh, which now houses the world’s largest refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, hosting over one million Rohingya refugees.

(L-R) Paul Reichler, Arsalan Suleman and Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow await the final judgment at the ICJ on 19 November 2026 (MEE)

Some of the survivors and witnesses were already sobbing as they entered the hall. 

Arsalan Suleman, the American lawyer who helped The Gambia bring the case and led its legal team, looked composed and greeted me with a confident smile.

The previous day, the court’s press team had shown journalists the two rooms the judges use before entering the courtroom.

In the Green Room, where they put on their black robes and white lace collars, a namecard stood on the table in front of each chair.

The judges then gather in the Red Room, beneath portraits of former court presidents. The press team also showed us the seating plan, so I knew Navi Pillay, the South African judge last month awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, would be the first judge through the door.

I was struck by how many reporters had turned up. The press room was full, so the court streamed the proceedings in its cafeteria. I had 10 minutes inside the courtroom to photograph the opening.

'La Cour!'

As we waited for the judges to enter, the room fell silent.

I turned my camera towards the judges’ entrance. Along the wood-panelled hall, four stained-glass windows by the Scottish artist Douglas Strachan depict war in reds and purples and a future at peace in blues and whites.  

“La Cour!” the usher called, prompting those inside the courtroom to stand as he opened the door. Above him hung Peace through Justice, Albert Besnard’s painting depicting a goddess of peace standing between two warring parties.

Pillay came through first, followed by the other 14 judges who make up the ICJ's bench, each of them to serve nine-year terms by UN member states.

The Gambia had chosen Pillay, a former UN human rights chief, to sit as an ad hoc judge in the case.

Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting peace and international law. Hours after the prize was announced on 9 October, the US announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was one of the first judges.

Navi Pillay enters the ICJ courtroom, 19 November 2026 (Reuters)

Also based in The Hague, the ICC prosecutes individuals for crimes including genocide.

Weeks before the Rohingya judgment, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, had accused Pillay of trying to lower the threshold for proving genocide in order to target Americans and their allies, and warned that Washington would be "watching" the proceedings closely. But Pillay appeared defiant as she led the judges into the hall.

At the UN’s International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the ad hoc court she also previously led, Pillay was one of three judges who convicted former Rwandan mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu in 1998.

It was the first time an international court found an individual guilty of genocide. Pillay led the drafting of the part of the judgment that established that rape and other forms of sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide, also a first under international law.

Most recently, she had chaired the UN’s independent commission of inquiry on occupied Palestine and Israel, which concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

On 19 November, with Pillay in the nine-to-six majority, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during its military’s horrific attacks on the group nine years earlier.

'We are very happy'

After the judgement, Suleman celebrated with Rohingya survivors and his colleagues, a silver garland around his neck. Others wore blue, golden, and silver garlands, in keeping with a Rohingya celebratory custom.

“We are very happy that finally we got a positive verdict, and we’ve got almost all of what we asked the court to deliver,” Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister and its representative before the court, told Middle East Eye. “This is unprecedented.”

The following day, at Suleman’s hotel a few minutes’ walk away from the Peace Palace, we spoke for an hour about how this extraordinary and unprecedented case came together - and the long and winding path to justice as circuitous as the Gambia river itself.

The Gambia team and Rohingya survivors celebrate after the ICJ delivered the genocide judgement (MEE)

Suleman is a Muslim American of Pakistani heritage, born and raised in New Orleans. He studied international security at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, before earning a master’s degree in international peace studies from Trinity College Dublin and then as law degree from Harvard Law School. 

Now a partner at the US law firm Foley Hoag, he previously served under President Barack Obama as acting US special envoy to the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), a group of 57 countries with its headquarters in Saudi Arabia that promotes cooperation among its members and aims to represent the interests of the world's Muslim-majority nations.

The relationships he built there helped him bring the idea for a case to The Gambia. 

From Bangladesh to The Hague

The case put mainland Africa’s smallest country, a Muslim-majority democracy on the Atlantic coast, at the centre of a landmark ruling on genocide.

The Gambia already has pedigree in the field of international justice. Its capital, Banjul, hosts the secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, and a former Gambian justice minister, Fatou Bensouda, went on to become chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia’s involvement in what would become the genocide case against Myanmar began in May 2018, when Bangladesh hosted a meeting of OIC foreign ministers in Dhaka.

The Rohingya crisis was on the agenda, including how to help the hundreds of thousands of refugees by then seeking safety in Bangladesh and hold those responsible for abuses in Myanmar to account.

The Gambia’s foreign minister was unable to attend the Dhaka meeting, Suleman said, so President Adama Barrow sent his justice minister, Abubacarr Tambadou, in his place. As part of the meeting, Bangladesh took delegates to the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, where Tambadou met Rohingya survivors.

Justice and accountability were already priorities at home. Gambians had voted out longtime ruler Yahya Jammeh in 2016 to end 22 years of authoritarian rule plagued by human rights abuses.

It had also taken a brief military intervention by Senegal, Nigeria and Ghana through the Ecowas bloc of West African states to force Jammeh to step down.

Barrow’s new government had made truth and reconciliation part of its mandate.

Tambadou had spent almost nine years prosecuting genocide at the UN’s Rwanda tribunal.

“So when he met the victims, he knew what he was seeing,” Suleman explained.

Abubacarr Tambadou, then Minister of Justice of The Gambia (R) waves to a representative of the Rohingya community prior to an interim ICJ ruling on 23 January 2020 (AFP)

Tambadou worked with OIC officials to set up a committee on accountability, which The Gambia chaired. 

Around the same time, Suleman and his colleagues at Foley Hoag were exploring whether a case could be brought under the Genocide Convention. When he raised the idea with former contacts at the OIC, one told him to speak to the Gambians.

Suleman met Tambadou in New York that September, during the UN General Assembly. Some early discussions had focused on international criminal tribunals, which prosecute individuals, Suleman recalled. 

The ICJ offered a way to hold Myanmar itself responsible. Tambadou invited him to present the committee with legal options in Banjul, the Gambian capital, the following February.

The committee backed an ICJ case, and the OIC’s foreign ministers and heads of state endorsed it.

The Gambia’s president and cabinet then approved bringing the case. The government appointed Suleman and his firm and filed its application on 11 November 2019. Suleman went on to lead the legal team. 

OIC members also helped pay for the case. In a statement issued after the judgment, the OIC Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed thanked a number of countries for their "generous financial contributions" including Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, Bangladesh, Kuwait, Nigeria, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Afghanistan.

Military coup

The Gambia first asked the court for emergency measures to protect the Rohingya while the case proceeded. 

In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar’s then civilian leader and herself a Nobel Peace Prize winner in 1991 during her long imprisonment by the military government, led the country’s delegation at the hearing.

The following month, the judges unanimously ordered Myanmar to take steps to prevent acts of genocide, preserve evidence and report on its compliance. The final judgment found that Myanmar breached the order to preserve evidence.

Myanmar challenged the court’s jurisdiction in January 2021, shortly before the military seized power from the elected civilian government.

The coup raised the question of who could speak for Myanmar. Suu Kyi could no longer represent the country, and both the military authorities and representatives of the ousted parliament claimed the right to do so.

Myanmar's then State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi (C) stands before the ICJ on 11 December 2019 (AFP)

Suleman said the dispute contributed to the delay. He said he understood why the years of waiting felt especially long to the Rohingya in the camps.

Myanmar argued that the OIC was the real applicant and that The Gambia had no right to bring the case. In July 2022, the court dismissed those objections.

The Gambia had filed in its own name. As a party to the Genocide Convention, it could hold another party to its obligations under the treaty. That right extended to countries whose own nationals had suffered no direct harm. 

How the lawyers built the case

Earlier UN investigations gave Suleman and his team a starting point and provided some of the key evidence the court relied on.

In March 2017, the UN Human Rights Council set up an independent fact-finding mission to investigate alleged abuses by Myanmar’s military and security forces, particularly in Rakhine State.

The following year the council created another body known as the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) with a different purpose: to collect, preserve and analyse evidence of serious international crimes and prepare case files for possible prosecutions.

The mission interviewed hundreds of Rohingya refugees and documented years of discrimination and hate speech, as well as mass killings, sexual violence and the destruction of villages.

The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide

Read More »

Suleman described the mission’s 2018 report as “the anchor around which the case could be built”.

Investigators looked at what happened before and after the attacks. 

Suleman described how troops went to villages in advance, forced residents to take down fences and confiscated items that could be used as weapons, including kitchen knives.

Investigators later used satellite data to document the destruction of villages. Burning them, Suleman said, destroyed evidence and made it harder for the Rohingya to return.

Most of the evidence went to the judges in written submissions running to hundreds of pages, backed by thousands more pages of documents. Those included statements from survivors gathered by organisations such as Legal Action Worldwide.

In the final judgment, the court found the fact-finding mission’s reports generally reliable, even though it used a lower standard of proof than the court.

Judges gave considerable weight to the IIMM’s detailed witness statements and reports because of its rigorous methods, and to satellite data that helped confirm accounts of villages being burned.

Witness statements collected by Legal Action Worldwide were also generally reliable, the judges found, though they carried less weight because they were less detailed. As Suleman explained, evidence given less weight could still help confirm another account.

At the January 2026 hearings, Suleman divided the arguments among the lawyers. Some covered the history of discrimination and the pattern of attacks. Others explained how the evidence, taken together, met the court’s standard for proving intent. Suleman’s oral intervention argued that the Myanmar military’s hate speech and propaganda helped show why the Rohingya were targeted.

The Gambia called a military expert, Michael Newton, to address Myanmar’s account of the operations. 

It also called three Rohingya survivors, who testified in closed sessions about what happened in their villages. Members of the legal team prepared them for questions from the judges and the possibility of cross-examination.

What persuaded the judges

The court found three forms of genocidal conduct proved: killing, causing serious physical or psychological harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births.

The judges found that Myanmar targeted about 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine State. That is roughly 58 percent of the 1.4 million Rohingya that Myanmar said lived in the country at the time.

The court found that the group targeted was large enough to constitute a “substantial part” of the Rohingya population under the Genocide Convention.

The judges said the evidence supported the UN fact-finding mission’s estimate of at least 10,000 deaths. But that was not the only factor that explained the genocidal campaign. The scale of the attacks also had to account for people who suffered serious physical or psychological harm or were subjected to measures intended to prevent births.

'The Gambia simply asked that the court apply its standard to the facts that The Gambia presented, and that’s what the court did'

- Arsalan Suleman, The Gambia's lawyer

Meanwhile, Myanmar claimed that its forces had passed up opportunities to kill more Rohingya, but the court responded that a finding of genocidal intent did not depend on whether the military had done everything it could to destroy the group.

In Min Gyi village, soldiers separated and executed men, killed children and opened fire on people trying to flee across a river.

The court held that the military’s sexual violence primarily targeted women and girls of reproductive age, including pregnant women in some cases.

The judges cited evidence that girls as young as seven were raped. Witnesses described children being shot or killed in burning homes. People who tried to escape across a river came under fire from soldiers. Some, particularly children and older people, drowned. 

The court’s finding that Myanmar took measures intended to prevent Rohingya births was based on restrictions on marriage and childbirth, the denial of birth registration to Rohingya children and the scale of the military’s sexual violence.

To provide genocidal intent, the ICJ applied the test it had used in earlier cases brought against Serbia by Croatia and Bosnia in relation to the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

The judges had to be fully convinced by the evidence that acts of genocide had occurred and that Myanmar’s forces intended to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part. Because the court was inferring intent from circumstantial evidence, genocidal intent had to be the only reasonable inference from the facts taken together. 

Myanmar argued that its campaign against the Rohingya was a counter-insurgency operation, and that other motives that could explain its conduct included a desire to drive the Rohingya out or to punish the civilian population.

But the court rejected all these explanations and said the “only reasonable inference” to be drawn from Myanmar’s conduct was genocide.

“The Gambia did not ask for any change in the standard,” Suleman said.

“The Gambia simply asked that the court apply its standard to the facts that The Gambia presented, and that’s what the court did.”

The Myanmar judgement also carries implications for other genocide cases before the court, most pressingly South Africa’s case against Israel over its conduct in Gaza.

“The court has shown that it will carefully consider the evidence of genocide in an impartial and holistic manner," said Suleman. "I expect that it will do so in all pending and future genocide cases.”

What it means for the Rohingya

For Suleman, one of the judgment’s most important conclusions was its recognition that the Rohingya had lived in Myanmar for generations and that it was their homeland.

The court ordered Myanmar to make it possible for displaced Rohingya to return safely, voluntarily and with dignity, to reunite families and to restore property or provide replacements. It also ordered guarantees against a recurrence and compensation for the harm done.

Myanmar has two years to report on restitution and on the amount and terms of compensation. The court will decide the amount and terms in a later phase.

The judges also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by people acting alongside its forces, failed to punish genocide and failed to enact legislation giving effect to the convention.

They ordered it to investigate suspects and, where warranted, prosecute and punish them.  

“We’re counting on their voluntary compliance,” Jallow, the justice minister, said.

If Myanmar fails to act, he said its bilateral partners and international organisations could use the binding judgment to press it to comply.

He also pointed to the UN Charter, which allows The Gambia to turn to the Security Council if Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling. The council would decide whether to act. 

Suleman said The Gambia intends to follow what Myanmar does over the next two years and press governments, the UN and regional bodies such as the OIC and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to help secure compliance.

“My role has not ended,” he said.

“The Gambia certainly intends to continue to ensure that this judgement is fully implemented.”

Turkish President Erdogan is expected to host the military leader in Ankara and may seek to bring him and his rival, Libyan Prime Minister Dbeibeh, together for talks in the future

Libya's Khalifa Haftar visits Moscow military airfield on 26 September 2023 (AFP/LNA)

Off

Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar is visiting Ankara on Tuesday, two Turkish sources familiar with the visit told Middle East Eye.

Reuters reported that Haftar arrived in the Turkish capital at the invitation of the Turkish government.

A Turkish source said Haftar would meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during the visit.

Over the past few years, Ankara has re-established ties with Haftar, eastern Libya’s de facto ruler and commander of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), and has developed particularly close ties with his son Saddam.

Libya’s eastern parliament approved a maritime delimitation agreement with Turkey last month, marking a new chapter in relations between Ankara and eastern Libya.

Tunc Demirtas, a regional expert at the Ankara-based think tank Seta, told MEE that Turkey may soon host Libyan Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, alongside Haftar, in an effort to bring the two sides closer together.

“Ankara is trying to reach its ‘One Libya’ objective, and these visits would be important to break through the deadlock,” Demirtas said.

He added that Erdogan is scheduled to visit Libya in December for the Turkey-Africa summit.

Haftar's forces execute 30 after secret military trials in eastern Libya

Read More »

Dbeibeh met Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin in Istanbul over the weekend. 

Demirtas said the recent spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war into waters near Libya underscored the need for stability in and around the country.

Such stability, he said, could come only through Libya’s unification.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Ukrainian forces had sunk a Russian corvette and a cargo ship off Libya’s western coast.

Turkey and the US have been trying to broker a merger between Libya’s rival military organisations, one based in Tripoli and the other in Benghazi.

An attempt to finalise the deal last month failed after the parties could not agree on a final draft.

Turkey and other countries in the region helped mediate a US-backed agreement that representatives of Libya’s rival political camps approved in Tripoli in August.

The agreement could pave the way for presidential and legislative elections within two years.

articles.title: Canadian ICC judge asks UK to release her funds frozen under US sanctions
articles.summary:
Canadian ICC judge asks UK to release her funds frozen under US sanctions

Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 10:17

Kimberly Prost says a wedding gift and a hotel payment were blocked for months, and that she lost access to Google Maps when she needed directions in London

Judge Kimberly Prost at the headquarters of the International Criminal Court on 28 April 2026 (ICC)

Off

International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Kimberly Prost has called on Britain to act after two payments she sent to the UK were frozen for months under US sanctions.

Prost said she had raised the transfers with British authorities and was considering asking whether the UK’s blocking statute could help her recover the money.

The Canadian judge said one transfer was a wedding gift for a young couple and the other was a hotel payment. Both were sent from the Netherlands in euros to Britain in pounds. A US bank’s UK branch became involved in both transactions, she said.

“In the United Kingdom, I have two instances where money was blocked and remains frozen,” Prost told journalists at the court’s headquarters in The Hague.

“And this is the scenario, money sent from here in the Netherlands in euros to the United Kingdom in pounds, and I get an email which says: ‘Your money has been blocked on the basis of the order of the President of the United States, and if you want your money back, you must apply to the Office of Foreign Assets Control in the United States for a licence.’”

In response to a request for comment, the UK foreign office did not address Prost's concerns. Instead, a source said that the UK "stands with the ICC" and is opposed to the sanctions. 

Her account sheds light on the personal toll of crippling US sanctions ahead of the ICC’s annual Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November.

The meeting was moved from New York over concerns that sanctions and visa restrictions would limit participation. Washington sanctioned the court itself on 9 October, after targeting individual judges and prosecutors.

'The fact that [the US is] applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated'

- Kimberly Prost, ICC judge

The meeting comes amid criticism that member states have failed to match their public support for the court with practical protection for officials such as Prost. 

Washington's sanctions and threats to the ICC have been prompted by the Trump administration's opposition to the court's arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the court's Afghanistan investigation which previously looked into US crimes. 

Washington has offered member states a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands to amend the court's treaty to prevent the prosecution of nationals of non-member states, like the US, Russia and Israel.

Once fully in effect in April, the sanctions could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations. 

Middle East Eye revealed on Monday that Guatemala had circulated a proposal urging talks with Washington on curbing the court’s ability to pursue nationals of countries outside the ICC, echoing US and Israeli demands. 

Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard accused Britain, Canada and other governments of seeking to appease Washington and called on them to act on their pledges to defend the court.

‘I have no regrets’

Washington sanctioned Prost in August 2025 over her role in a 2020 appeals ruling that authorised an investigation in Afghanistan, which could cover alleged crimes by US personnel.

Asked about a recent decision to close that investigation and open a separate inquiry focused on the Taliban, Prost said she had questions about the decision herself and would wait to see the outcome of the appeal lodged by the Office of the Prosecutor against the decision.

“I was sanctioned on the basis of my participation in the Appeals Chamber decision [to open the Afghanistan investigation], which I would make again today on the basis of the evidence that was in front of the Chamber,” she said. “I don’t know the state of the evidence today, only the prosecutor does. And I have no regrets about that decision whatsoever.”

Kimberly Prost, ICC judge, speaks to journalists at the court's headquarters in The Hague on 19 November 2026 (MEE/Sondos Asem)

Prost said the sanctions had left her without a credit card, made online shopping nearly impossible and stopped her from using Google Maps when she needed directions in London.

She said, however, she is undeterred and that the pressure had no bearing on her work.

“Independently and objectively, we look at the facts, the evidence, apply the law, and that’s the basis for our decision,” she said. “So the fact that they’re applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated.”

She is one of three ICC judges who have sued the Trump administration over the sanctions.

‘Clear red lines’

Prost said British authorities had treated the frozen transfers as a decision for private industry.

She disputed that the bank was obliged to block the funds and said she was considering asking about Britain’s blocking statute, a mechanism designed to counter certain foreign sanctions.

Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands

Read More »

Britain was among nine countries that publicly opposed the October sanctions against the court.

“Now, in addition to those reactions and to the diplomacy, we need some strong measures being taken,” she said.

She urged governments to use legal tools to tackle overcompliance and called for more public support from civil society and judicial associations.

Prost, who helped negotiate the Rome Statute for Canada in 1998, said she supported dialogue with Washington but warned against putting the court’s jurisdiction up for negotiation. She was speaking about possible talks in general, without addressing Guatemala’s proposal specifically.

“I mean, to me, that decision to include territorial jurisdiction was at the heart of the Rome Statute, and, in addition, it’s the will of those who participated in negotiations,” she said. “You can’t just change that because a group of states decide that it’s inconvenient at this point in time.”

Under that principle, the court can pursue certain crimes committed on the territory of a member state regardless of the suspect’s nationality. Guatemala’s paper floated requiring the consent of the suspect’s country even when the alleged crimes took place in a member state.

“One thing that cannot happen is this court cannot [be made to] stop,” Prost said.

Barzani rejects Baghdad’s orders to take over Kurdish oil fields and border crossings

Kurdish regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani has called Baghdad’s move to assume authority over oil fields and border crossings in four provinces “completely unacceptable”.

“We were dismayed by the statement issued today because it goes against the talks we have held with Baghdad’s authorities,” Barzani said, according to Rudaw.

His remarks followed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s instructions today for federal authorities to run the region’s border crossings after an investigation into oil smuggling.

Al-Zaidi tasked the Oil Ministry with overseeing Kurdish-controlled fields across four provinces and barred the Kurdistan Regional Government from authorising oil exports.

He also dismissed Kirkuk’s border crossings authority head and police chief, saying they had failed to pursue the smuggling case.

Doha is maintaining contact with Tehran and Washington as it works to mediate between them, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari says.

articles.title: Iran says fourth tanker hits mine in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary:
Iran says fourth tanker hits mine in Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says another tanker has hit a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the reported total to four. It said the ship took an “unauthorised” passage.

The IRGC Navy’s public relations office previously reported that mine explosions set three vessels ablaze, according to Iran’s IRNA news agency.

Strikes against ships crossing without Iranian approval have increased sharply over recent weeks as Tehran seeks to enforce its asserted control over the shipping route.

Cairo has designated 35 Muslim associations across Europe as terrorists, months after an Israeli ministry report singled out many of the same names

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi (left) speaks with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden (right) and European Council President Antonio Costa at a dinner in Brussels after the EU-Egypt summit on 22 October 2025 (Simon Wohlfahrt/Pool/AFP)

Off

In September, Egyptian police arrested all six journalists at Matsadaash, a news platform dedicated to fact-checking and investigative reporting. They were accused of spreading misinformation on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, a charge the outlet denies.

The authorities then turned on Mada Masr, one of Egypt's best-known independent news sites. In October, a court ordered the site closed. The following month, its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, faced a retrial on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The same charges brought her a one-year prison sentence in absentia in 2024.

Shaher Ayyad, an editorial board member at the news site al-Manassa, told Reuters: "Independent outlets are often portrayed as lawbreakers or enemies of the state."

Both cases are part of the repression that Amnesty International detailed in its 2025 report, which found that authorities "continued to criminalize dissenting forms of expression and peaceful assembly, targeting journalists, protesters, opposition politicians and others who criticized the government's human rights record or called for political change".

Egypt's record of abuse at home has long been documented. A decade after the former military chief took power, the US State Department's 2024 human rights report called the situation dire.

The department cited credible reports of "torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment; arbitrary arrest and detention", "instances of transnational repression against individuals in another country" and "serious restrictions on freedom of expression and media freedom, including unjustified arrests or prosecutions of journalists and censorship".

The list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions

On 10 November, Egypt went a step further and published a list of 35 associations and 36 individuals that the Cairo Criminal Court has designated as "terrorists".

Strikingly, the list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions, the national, cultural, educational and religious bodies that serve Muslim communities across 27 countries.

At its centre is the Council of European Muslims, formerly the Federation of Islamic Organisations in Europe, an umbrella body founded in 1989 whose members help Muslims practise their faith, preserve their identity and integrate into their societies.

The designations are valid for five years, subject to appeal, extension and removal. They were published just days after Egyptian authorities placed the Muslim Brotherhood permanently on the country's terrorism list, replacing a series of time-limited designations.

For those named, the practical consequences could include restrictions on travel and banking, and a real threat to their personal security.

A European echo

Egypt's latest move has raised fears that it is exporting its crackdown on political dissent and extending its hunt for the Muslim Brotherhood, the movement that won the country's election in 2012 before being ousted the following year by the then defence minister, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

Anas Altikriti, the British-Iraqi founder of the Cordoba Foundation and one of the 36 individuals named, said Arab governments regard the political influence of Muslim communities in the West as a threat. "What you actually do is to shut down Muslim civil society in the West," he told The New Arab.

The Brotherhood bogeyman: How Europe and the US criminalise Muslim civic life

Read More »

In 2014, three years after the Arab Spring uprisings, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others, also designated the Brotherhood a "terrorist organisation".

The list was also published a month after the European Parliament's largest group, the European People's Party, pushed through a non-binding resolution "on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network".

The resolution had support from fellow conservatives, the far right and liberals, and opposition from the social democrats, the Greens and the left.

It explicitly named the Council of European Muslims, along with other Muslim and anti-racist organisations, and called for groups associated with the council to be denied access to EU institutions and removed from the EU's transparency register.

Amnesty International and more than 100 other civil society groups wrote to European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in protest, but the letter has gone unanswered.

Given that those targeted are based in Europe, there is reason to suspect a concerted effort by political forces seeking to criminalise Muslim and anti-racist civic life. The picture, however, is bigger than that.

The global picture

It is a mistake to treat Cairo's terror list as a purely domestic decision, or even a Euro-Arab one. Egypt is better understood as part of a wider geopolitical strategy, the culmination of developments well beyond its borders.

First, Egypt has long wanted the Muslim Brotherhood on western terrorist lists, and some argue Sisi is acting largely on behalf of one of Egypt's main financiers, the UAE.

Second, it is no coincidence that those efforts gained ground under the second Trump administration. In November 2025, the president set in motion the designation of Brotherhood chapters, including Egypt's, as terrorist organisations by executive order rather than legislation.

That gave the Egyptian president the symbolic backing to keep telling a story that looks domestic at first glance.

The UAE, for its part, listed 15 civil society groups in the US and Europe as terrorist organisations in 2014, alongside armed groups such as al-Qaeda, Boko Haram and the Islamic State group.

They included the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights group in the US, and the forerunner of the Council of European Muslims, along with the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium that Cairo has now designated.

Muslim Brotherhood allegations are not a new invention, and they played a major role in November's US midterms, where they were levelled at Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.

In January 2025, the UAE added eight companies registered in the UK and owned by Emirati dissidents and their relatives.

The Israel connection

In February 2026, nine months before Egypt published its list, the Netanyahu government's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism released a report titled "The Muslim Brotherhood Across Europe".

The ministry makes no secret of its purpose. Its report says the ministry "systematically documents activities by those engaged in delegitimization" of Israel, and lists "cooperation with pro-Palestinian organizations" and the promotion of boycotts, sanctions and divestment among its areas of focus.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence

Its research department identified nine "key organizations in Europe".

Three of them appear among the eight Europe-wide associations on the Egyptian court's list: the Council of European Muslims, the European Council for Fatwa and Research, and the European Institute of Human Sciences. The Council of European Muslims is the first organisation named in both documents.

The Israeli ministry's report presents the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium as part of the Brotherhood's European network, and all four are now on Egypt's list. Nearly a third of the 36 individuals the Egyptian court named also appear in the report, including four men it identifies as presidents of the council.

A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence. It suggests Cairo is working from a script written elsewhere, further reducing the country that once led the Arab world to the role of a vessel for wealthy backers aligned with Israel.

Ukrainian foreign minister advises Putin to stop complaining about strikes on oil refineries and end war instead
articles.summary:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has responded to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin's complaints about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, advising him to order an end to the war instead.

Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter)

Quote: "If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war."

Details: Sybiha added that if Putin does not want his warships to come under attack, he can order the war to stop.

"Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," the foreign minister wrote.

Earlier, Putin complained that Ukraine is attacking Russian oil refineries despite a direct request from US President Donald Trump to refrain from strikes, and promised retaliation.

Background:

In September, Trump said that he had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to scale back strikes on Russian oil refineries, and that Zelenskyy had supposedly agreed.

In early October, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries, provided that Russian forces stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Belarusian leader says he could fly to Putin with Zelenskyy on same plane
articles.summary:
Self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko has offered to become Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's "security guarantor" and fly with him to Moscow.

Source: Lukashenko in an interview with French weekly news magazine Le Point on 17 November, as reported by Belarusian state-owned news outlet BelTA

Details: Russian leader Vladimir Putin previously invited Zelenskyy to visit Moscow, but the Ukrainian president refused. Lukashenko has now proposed his own version of the trip.

Quote: "Volodymyr Zelenskyy and I could get on a plane and fly to Moscow. Just the two of us. I could get on a plane with him and fly to Moscow as his security guarantor."

Details: The Belarusian leader believes that the three of them would reach an agreement to end the war more quickly than they would with Europeans.

Quote: "In any case, the three of us will determine what our future will look like – that of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. We are three Slavic nations. Our role will be decisive. Here, in this region, the three main Slavic nations have historically determined, and will continue to determine, how we live."

Details: When the journalist pointed out that Zelenskyy would not agree to such a format for negotiations, Lukashenko replied: "If he does not agree, let him fight. Let him go to the front line himself with a rifle and fight. The war is ongoing and must be stopped. And we could reach an agreement."

Lukashenko also claimed that Russia is winning on the battlefield.

Background:

The Financial Times previously reported that the Trump administration had told European and Ukrainian officials that it wants Ukraine and Russia to reach a peace agreement by the beginning of January 2027.

On 23 November, US special envoy Jared Kushner said that US negotiators will work with representatives of Ukraine, the European Union and Russia in the coming weeks to reach a common agreement on security architecture.

articles.title: Ukraine's National Guard destroys 22 pieces of Russian military equipment in one operation – video
articles.summary:
Fighters from the National Guard's separate special-purpose unit, Lasar's Group, have struck and destroyed more than 20 pieces of Russian military equipment in Zaporizhzhia Oblast in a single special operation. Fourteen of them were tanks.

Source: Lasar's Group on Facebook; Ukrainska Pravda

Quote: "Since 2022, the key objective of the Lasar's Group special unit of Ukraine's National Guard has been to destroy Russian military equipment. This applies particularly to tanks, which have caused huge problems for infantry. In almost five years, we have destroyed more than 2,400 tanks and continue to hunt them successfully, as we did during our recent special operation."

Details: Lasar's Group fighters identified 22 pieces of Russian military equipment deep behind the line of contact in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Analysts gathered intelligence on the area where the equipment was concentrated, after which aerial reconnaissance was carried out. The reconnaissance drone crews of Lasar's Group provided precise information on the location of the Russian equipment.

The unit's strike drones were then deployed deep into Russian-held territory.

The operation, which took place last night, according to Ukrainska Pravda, resulted in the destruction of two tanks and a lorry.

The following equipment was struck:

12 tanks

two command and staff vehicles

two pieces of engineering equipment

three lorries.

Quote: "The entire special operation was carried out by Lasar's Group, and the total damage inflicted on the enemy amounts to tens of millions of dollars. The Russians should remember: no matter how many tanks they manufacture, we will burn them all."

Background: Earlier, fighters from Lasar's Group destroyed a Russian Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun and missile system in the temporarily occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, setting it on fire by dropping munitions from a heavy bomber drone.

articles.title: Hungarian PM says he hosted refugees from Zakarpattia Oblast
articles.summary:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said that he hosted refugees from Zakarpattia Oblast after the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.

Source: Magyar at a joint press briefing with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Uzhhorod, as reported by European Pravda

Details: During his first visit to Zakarpattia Oblast as prime minister, Magyar stressed that Hungary condemns Russian aggression against Ukraine and is providing humanitarian aid to its neighbouring country in every way possible.

The prime minister added that his country has provided shelter to tens of thousands of refugees from Ukraine, many of whom are ethnic Hungarians from Zakarpattia Oblast. He said that he had also personally taken in young people from the oblast after the start of the Russian invasion.

Background:

Magyar noted that he had not come to Uzhhorod empty-handed and announced an aid package for Zakarpattia Oblast, which includes medical equipment, generators and vehicles.

On 24 November, Magyar was making his first visit to Ukraine as Hungary's prime minister.

During the visit, he said that significant progress had been made in talks with the Ukrainian side on 10 issues concerning the linguistic, cultural and educational rights of the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine.

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: "Categorical objection": Ukrainian government responds to appointment of Russian official to senior IAEA post
articles.summary:
Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Energy have expressed deep outrage over the decision by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi to appoint Russian official Aleksei Ferapontov, who is under sanctions, as his deputy.

Source: a joint statement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Energy

Details: Ferapontov previously served as deputy head of Russia's Federal Service for Environmental, Technological and Nuclear Supervision (Rostekhnadzor).

He was involved in the illegal seizure of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and the imposition of Russian regulatory control over it. Ukraine imposed personal sanctions on him on 12 February 2023 for this.

"The appointment of a representative of a state body directly involved in undermining the principles of nuclear safety to one of the IAEA's highest leadership positions is fundamentally at odds with the Agency's mandate," the statement said.

The Ukrainian side has repeatedly stressed to the IAEA leadership, both through diplomatic channels and in previous public statements by the heads of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Energy, that such an appointment is categorically unacceptable.

The ministries said that this personnel decision runs counter to the principles and standards set out in Article VII of the IAEA Statute.

The article establishes the highest standards of professional competence and integrity as the primary criteria for staff selection, and guarantees the independence of the director general and IAEA staff from external influence.

"Such an appointment also runs counter to the spirit and objectives of resolutions adopted by the IAEA General Conference and Board of Governors on nuclear safety, nuclear security and safeguards in Ukraine.

An international organisation whose mission is to protect the world from nuclear threats cannot grant leadership powers to representatives of state bodies involved in creating those threats," the Ukrainian government stressed.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Energy have lodged a categorical objection against this unacceptable personnel decision and demanded its immediate reversal.

They also called on IAEA member states, particularly members of the Board of Governors, to issue a clear public assessment of the appointment and activate the mechanisms provided for in the Agency's Statute to review the decision.

Background: On 17 November, it emerged that Grossi planned to appoint Ferapontov as his deputy. Greenpeace International called on him to refrain from making the appointment.

articles.title: Putin complains that Ukraine is striking Russian oil refineries despite Trump's request and vows retaliation
articles.summary:
Russian ruler Vladimir Putin has complained that Ukraine is attacking Russian oil refineries despite a direct request from US President Donald Trump to refrain from strikes, and has promised retaliation.

Source: Russian news agency Interfax

Quote from Putin: "We see that the Kyiv regime is continuing its attacks on our refining facilities. By the way, despite the US president's appeal and direct request not to do this and to refrain from these attacks, the Kyiv authorities are not heeding such advice."

Details: Putin noted that "everything is continuing as if nothing had happened".

"In this regard, I would like to note that appropriate action on our part is inevitable. Everyone should be aware of this," the Kremlin leader said at a meeting of the Commission on the Development Strategy of the Fuel and Energy Sector on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Putin sought to argue that the "escalation launched by the adversary in early June this year and intended, as publicly stated, to last 40 days" is supposedly incapable of causing critical damage to Russia.

Background:

In September, Trump said that he had asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to scale back strikes on Russian oil refineries, and that Zelenskyy had supposedly agreed.

In early October, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries, provided that Russian forces stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Hungarian PM announces aid for Zakarpattia Oblast during visit to Uzhhorod
articles.summary:
Hungary has sent an aid package to Zakarpattia Oblast, which includes medical equipment, generators and vehicles.

Source: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar during his visit to Uzhhorod, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Magyar emphasised that the aid is intended to meet the needs of Zakarpattia Oblast.

"And today we have not come empty-handed, as we have brought aid for Zakarpattia. This includes an expensive device for monitoring patients' condition, medicines, energy equipment, including generators worth millions of forints, as well as vehicles," he said.

The prime minister also announced the establishment of a separate social support programme.

Quote: "And here, in the presence of the president, I would like to announce that today the Hungarian parliament decided at its session to increase the fund for supporting Hungarians abroad by billions of forints. We are establishing a special Ilona Zrínyi Social Fund, through which this aid will be provided."

Background:

On 24 November, Magyar was making his first visit to Ukraine as Hungary's prime minister.

During the visit, he said that significant progress had been made in talks with the Ukrainian side on 10 issues concerning the linguistic, cultural and educational rights of the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine.

Magyar had previously said that he would meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders of the Hungarian community during the visit.

The prime minister added that he and Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán would visit several Hungarian institutions.

articles.title: Estonia sending signal to Ukraine not to pollute Baltic Sea – Estonian PM
articles.summary:
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal has said that his country will not allow anyone, including Ukraine, to use its airspace, sea or land for attacks, adding that Kyiv will be sent a signal regarding the risk of environmental pollution threatening the Baltic Sea if Ukraine attacks oil tankers in the region.

Source: European Pravda, citing Estonian public broadcaster ERR

Details: The Estonian prime minister noted that Estonia's land and maritime territories are closed to attacks on other vessels, including oil tankers.

Michal said Estonia had told its allies, including Ukraine, that it does not share its airspace, sea or land and that no one else can use them. He added that Ukraine will definitely be sent a signal about the risk of environmental pollution, noting that Kyiv has likely already received it at a level lower than heads of state, but that it will certainly be repeated.

According to the prime minister, however, it must be taken into account that Ukrainian attacks on Russia's shadow fleet and infrastructure will continue, as these vessels are key to financing the Kremlin's war machine and transporting weapons.

He said one should not assume that these attacks on Russian infrastructure or Russian ships in the Baltic Sea or any other sea will be the last. Since nearly half of Putin's war funding comes from those very ships, and they also carry weapons, Michal said he would not assume they will not be attacked again at some point.

However, Kristen Michal stressed that damage to tankers in poor technical condition poses a threat to the Baltic Sea.

The Estonian prime minister added that some shadow fleet vessels were in poor condition and could be damaged and leak. Referring to the latest vessel, Sparta II, as well as all other ships at risk or already hit, he said a potential oil spill is a serious threat to the state of the Baltic Sea and must be addressed.

Background:

On Saturday 21 November, the Finnish defence forces detected a drone attack on a Russian merchant vessel west of Suursaari in international waters in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish Border Guard stated that the Russian vessel was struck by Ukrainian drones on 21 November.

articles.title: Ukraine's defence minister announces major air defence agreements with Norway
articles.summary:
Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara has held a meeting in Oslo with Norwegian Defence Minister Tore O. Sandvik, following which he announced agreements to strengthen Ukraine's air defence.

Source: press service of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, as reported by European Pravda

Details: During the meeting, the ministers held substantive discussions on support for Ukraine over the winter period and throughout 2027.

In particular, bilateral aid from Norway next year will amount to at least US$7 billion. It will primarily focus on priority areas: strengthening air defence and unmanned systems.

Khmara said they had considered options for supplying Ukraine with assets to protect its skies, including interceptor missiles for air defence systems, noting that significant and important agreements had been reached for Ukraine.

Separately, the ministers discussed a project to integrate different types of missiles into the NASAMS systems operated by Ukraine.

They also discussed ways to supply additional combat aircraft and ammunition for them.

In addition, Khmara outlined the main areas for developing cooperation between Ukraine and Norway, including the exchange of combat experience and the development of joint ventures, where the two countries already have practical groundwork.

Background:

Earlier, it emerged that the Ukrainian and Norwegian defence industries had developed a new type of air defence system – Desna – which is already helping protect Ukraine from drones.

In addition, as part of Khmara's visit to Oslo, the ministers of the two countries signed a memorandum of intent regarding the testing of Ukraine's Delta combat digital ecosystem.

articles.title: Sweden announces winter support package for Ukraine
articles.summary:
The Swedish government announced a winter aid package for Ukraine on Tuesday 24 November. The assistance is aimed at strengthening Ukraine's resilience and meeting urgent needs, the government said.

Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by the Swedish government

Details: The winter package consists of SEK 155 million (€13.8 million) for the Ukrainian Red Cross, SEK 85 million (€7.6 million) to support the energy sector and a procurement mandate worth SEK 300 million (€26.7 million) for the civil defence agency.

Swedish Acting Minister for Foreign Trade Benjamin Dousa noted that Russia's brutal attacks on Ukraine's population and civilian infrastructure are a deliberate attempt to make the winter unbearable. He said millions of people risk being left without electricity, heating and water during another wartime winter that could be the worst yet, which is why Sweden is supporting the energy sector and families living near the front line.

He also added that the Swedish government is ensuring continued deliveries of equipment to protect energy facilities from Russian attacks.

Sweden's support for the Ukrainian Red Cross will be used, among other things, for cash assistance to vulnerable households, heating, generators and other essential relief measures.

The €7.6 million in energy assistance is being provided through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and will go towards equipment and installations that strengthen the energy supply.

The €26.7 million procurement mandate granted to the Swedish civil defence agency is aimed at ensuring uninterrupted deliveries of emergency equipment from Sweden to Ukraine throughout the winter.

Background:

It was also reported that Denmark will allocate an extraordinary €20 million grant to support Ukraine's energy sector.

In late October, the Norwegian government announced an allocation of NOK 500 million (€48 million) in energy support for Ukraine ahead of winter.

articles.title: Moldova proposes reviving Prut River navigation with Romania, strengthening links with Ukraine
articles.summary:
Moldova has put forward a proposal to Romania regarding the development of river infrastructure and the relaunch of navigation along the Prut River, strengthening transport links with Ukraine.

Source: European Pravda, citing Moldovan news outlet NewsMaker

Details: The plans to develop navigation on the Prut will start with a pilot section between the ports of Giurgiulești and Galați. The initiative aims to develop river transport, ensure effective water resource management, expand irrigation systems, and strengthen transport links between Moldova, Romania and Ukraine.

Mircea Păscăluță, State Secretary at Moldova's Ministry of Regional Development, said Moldova supports the idea of resuming navigation on the Prut and is confident that this could bring a great deal to the region: closer ties between communities on both banks, new opportunities for farmers and businesses, and "an increasingly natural convergence with the European space".

The resumption of navigation on the Prut is envisaged in Moldova's Mobility Strategy 2030 and bilateral agreements with Bucharest. The two countries discussed joint work to implement the project in Chișinău in January this year.

In the first phase, Moldova proposes to conduct joint hydrographic surveys, analyse the economic potential of freight transport, and assess the environmental impact.

Next, the two countries could develop a pilot section in the lower reaches of the Prut with direct access to the ports of Giurgiulești and Galați in order to test a mechanism for joint financing and fairway maintenance before expanding infrastructure upstream.

In the long term, the project envisages developing around 500 km of navigable waterway and integrating it into a future river corridor linking the Baltic and Black Seas.

Background:

Earlier, Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan urged Ukrainian businesses to use Moldova's railway to export goods to Romania.

It was also reported that freight traffic to the European Union has increased significantly at all customs posts on the Moldovan-Romanian border, partly due to exports from Ukraine.

articles.title: Russians strike business in Rivne Oblast
articles.summary:
Russian forces have attacked the Sarny district in Rivne Oblast, hitting a business. Early reports indicate that no one was injured.

Source: Oleksandr Koval, Head of Rivne Oblast Military Administration, on Telegram

Quote: "A civilian business was targeted by the enemy during yet another attack on the Sarny district. A fire broke out in one of the premises."

Details: Koval said firefighters and other emergency services are already working at the scene.

Earlier, Koval reported that the northern part of Rivne Oblast came under attack in the morning, with the Russians targeting energy facilities.

Background:

On the morning of 24 November, Russian forces struck a critical infrastructure facility in Vinnytsia.

A Russian UAV attacked Korosten railway station. One person was killed by debris and two others were injured.

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine needs €115bn for 2027, with €90bn currently agreed
articles.summary:
Ukraine needs €115 billion to withstand the challenges of 2027. Agreements have so far been reached with European partners to secure €90 billion, while a further €25 billion still needs to be found.

Source: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's address to participants of a meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities

Quote: "Next year, Ukraine needs at least €115 billion to hold firm. We already had 45 billion thanks to last year's decision by the European Union to provide 45 billion a year for two years.

Recently, we agreed on additional funding – an additional 45 billion. So we understand that Ukraine will receive €90 billion next year. The European Commission has already presented a way to secure this funding, and we are now working to ensure that the European Union supports it. We need to find another 25 billion. I am confident that we will accomplish this task."

Details: Zelenskyy added that in the current fifth year of the full-scale war Ukraine has managed to ensure a financial foundation for the country and its people.

Background:

In October, Zelenskyy appealed to EU leaders to provide Ukraine with at least an additional €70 billion in aid next year for defence, weapons and strengthening resilience. "The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you – for defence, for weapons and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," the president said.

On 18 November, the European Commission adopted a package of legislative proposals to provide Ukraine with up to €45 billion in additional financial support in 2027, on top of the €45 billion planned under the €90 billion loan.

articles.title: Zelenskyy and Hungarian PM Magyar honour fallen Ukrainian defenders in Uzhhorod – video
articles.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar have met in Uzhhorod and honoured the memory of Ukraine's fallen defenders.

Source: Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform from the scene, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Zelenskyy and Magyar laid flowers at the memorial to Ukraine's fallen defenders on the Hill of Glory in Uzhhorod.

Background:

On 24 November, Magyar made the first visit to Zakarpattia in the capacity of Hungarian prime minister since 2015.

He had previously said that during the visit he would meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as well as leaders of the Hungarian community in Zakarpattia.

Magyar added that together with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, he will visit several Hungarian institutions.

articles.title: Russians strike Dnipro: high-rise building damaged, four injured
articles.summary:
Russian forces have attacked the city of Dnipro, injuring local residents and damaging a high-rise residential building.

Source: Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, on Telegram

Quote: "The enemy has attacked Dnipro... At least four people have been injured."

Details: Hanzha initially reported damage to a high-rise building, and information about the casualties emerged later.

"Medics are providing them with the necessary assistance," Hanzha noted.

Background: Earlier, it was reported that on 23 November, a Russian drone attacked a vehicle belonging to DTEK while energy workers were inspecting power lines in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
